pl-l3d24c3-d1e115.summary: Poses the question: if faith concerns non-apparent and unseen things, is it only about the unknown? If so, it would seem to concern only what is entirely ignored.
claims: If faith concerns only the unknown, it would concern what is wholly ignored.

pl-l3d24c3-d1e118.summary: Distinguishes exterior and interior vision: faith is not of things subject to exterior sight, but can concern things somehow grasped by interior vision, some understood in part (though not as in the future), others not. Since faith comes from hearing (interior as well as exterior), it cannot be of what is wholly unknown; with Augustine, faith pertains to the heart, not to any bodily sense. Some things believed are understood by natural reason, others not.
claims: Faith does not concern objects of bodily sight.
Faith can concern things grasped by interior vision.
Faith comes from hearing and cannot be about the wholly unknown.
Faith belongs to the heart, not to a bodily sense.
Some objects of faith are understood by natural reason, others are not.

pl-l3d24c3-d1e133.summary: Isaiah ('unless you believe, you will not understand') and Augustine distinguish things not believed unless understood from things not understood unless believed. Yet no one can believe into God without understanding something, since faith comes from hearing preaching.
claims: Some things must be understood before being believed; others believed before being understood.
Believing into God requires some understanding.

pl-l3d24c3-d1e146.summary: Augustine (De Trinitate): certain faith somehow begins knowledge, but certain knowledge is perfected only after this life.
claims: Faith begins knowledge; perfect knowledge comes only after this life.

pl-l3d24c3-d1e155.summary: Ambrose: where there is faith, there is not immediately knowledge; where there is knowledge, faith has preceded.
claims: Faith precedes knowledge but does not immediately bring it.

pl-l3d24c3-d1e164.summary: Lombard concludes from the authorities that some things are believed that are not understood or known unless first believed, while some things are sometimes understood even before they are believed.
claims: Some things are understood only after being believed.
Some things can be understood before being believed.

pl-l3d24c3-d1e167.summary: Adds that present understanding is not like future knowledge; and faith itself increases understanding now, since faith purifies hearts, and without loving God through faith the heart is not cleansed to know him.
claims: Present understanding falls short of future knowledge.
Faith purifies the heart and thereby increases understanding.
The heart is cleansed to know God only through faith-filled love.

pl-l3d24c3-d1e170.summary: Augustine: to know God is to behold him with the mind and grasp him firmly; but before the heart can perceive God as the pure in heart do, it must be cleansed through faith-filled love. Lombard underlines that God cannot be known unless first believed with love.
claims: To know God is to behold and firmly grasp him with the mind.
The heart is fit to see God only after being cleansed by loving faith.
God cannot be known unless first believed with love.

pl-l3d24c3-d1e179.summary: Synthesizes: since no one can believe into God without understanding something, some objects of faith cannot be known unless first believed, some cannot be believed unless first understood, and faith further increases understanding. Things believed before being understood are not wholly unknown, since faith comes from hearing; they are partly unknown because not known with science. What is believed is unknown, but not entirely, just as one can love what one does not know.
claims: Some things must be believed before they are known, others understood before they are believed.
Faith increases understanding.
What is believed before being understood is partly but not wholly unknown.
Belief and love can be directed to what is partially unknown.

pl-l3d24c3-d1e183.summary: Augustine asks whether what is unknown can be loved; if not, no one loves God before knowing him. But faith, hope, and charity exist in a soul believing what it does not yet know and hoping for and loving what it believes. Hence what is not known is loved, yet it is believed.
claims: One can love what one does not yet know, provided it is believed.
Faith, hope, and charity exist in a soul that believes what it does not yet know.

pl-l3d24c3.summary: Considers whether faith, being of the unseen, concerns only what is wholly unknown. Distinguishing exterior from interior vision, Lombard holds that faith is not about objects of bodily sight but can concern things grasped by interior vision. Some things believed are understood by natural reason, others are not; some must be understood before they are believed, others believed before they are understood, and faith further increases understanding by purifying the heart. What is believed before being understood is not wholly unknown, just as one can love what one does not fully know; full knowledge comes only after this life.
claims: Faith does not concern objects of exterior vision but can concern objects of interior vision.
Faith comes from hearing and so cannot be about what is entirely unknown.
Some things believed are understood by natural reason; others are not.
Some things must be understood to be believed; others must be believed to be understood.
Faith purifies the heart and thereby increases understanding of God.
What is believed is partly unknown, but not wholly, as what is loved may be partly unknown.
Certain knowledge of God is perfected only after this life.
